analysis.one_liner: Requires employers, governments, and businesses to make their websites and apps accessible to people with disabilities.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The ADA was written in 1990, before websites and apps existed, and courts disagree over whether it covers them. This bill would require employers, government agencies, public accommodations, and testing services to make their websites and applications usable by people with disabilities, including businesses that operate only online. The Justice Department and the EEOC would write one uniform accessibility standard, update it every three years, and enforce it alongside private lawsuits by disabled users.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 1 in 4 American adults living with a disability. The bill's findings note that most websites and apps contain barriers that screen-reader users, blind, deaf, and mobility-impaired users cannot get past, excluding them from jobs, government services, education, and shopping that everyone else reaches through a screen.

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered entities to make websites and applications 'perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust' for users with disabilities, with the same privacy, independence, and ease of use as everyone else, and applies the rule even to businesses with no physical location [S3].

Directs the Justice Department and the EEOC to issue proposed accessibility rules within 12 months and final standards within 24 months of enactment, replacing today's situation where courts split over whether the ADA covers websites at all [S3].

Enforcement comes from DOJ, the EEOC, and private civil suits that do not require exhausting administrative remedies first; prevailing plaintiffs can seek compensatory and punitive damages and recover attorney's fees [S3].

Creates a standing advisory committee whose majority must be people with disabilities, a technical assistance center funded at $15 million a year to help entities comply, and a National Council on Disability study of emerging technologies [S3].
Bars regulators from adopting any rule requiring a disabled person to give advance notice before filing a lawsuit, keeping private enforcement open [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses, government agencies, and web development companies, which would bear the cost of auditing, redesigning, and maintaining accessible websites and apps. Entities can escape liability if compliance would impose an 'undue burden' or fundamentally alter what they provide, a defense aimed mainly at smaller operations.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on thousands of businesses, schools, and agencies; the bill acknowledges this by writing an 'undue burden' defense into every covered category, but what counts as undue would be fought case by case [S3].

The bill prohibits any regulation requiring a would-be plaintiff to notify a business of an accessibility problem before suing, preserving strong private enforcement but leaving entities exposed to suits without a chance to fix the problem first [S3].

The government is authorized at only $5 million a year for rulemaking and enforcement and $15 million a year for technical assistance, so the burden of adapting falls primarily on private compliance spending rather than public help [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of Americans who cannot use inaccessible websites, this was a significant civil rights measure: it would have replaced conflicting court rulings with one enforceable national standard. The costs are real but ordinary for disability accommodation, and the bill's undue-burden defense and technical assistance center were designed to cushion small entities. The main design risk is litigation volume, which the drafters accepted by refusing a notice requirement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee the day it was introduced and died there, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Duckworth introduced the Websites and Software Applications Accessibility Act on September 28, 2022, joined by original cosponsors Sen. Robert Casey, Sen. Brian Schatz, and Sen. Edward Markey [S1, S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; that is the last action of any kind in the record [S5].
Five senators cosponsored the bill in total: four Senate Democrats and one Independent. No Republican signed on [S4].
The HELP Committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses with inaccessible websites and the developers who build them avoided new federal accessibility standards and the risk of damages and attorney's fees in private lawsuits. Internet users with disabilities remain without a uniform right to access, still relying on conflicting court decisions.

for.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and chaired the effort; she is a disabled veteran and long-time disability rights advocate.

for.name: Sens. Robert Casey, Brian Schatz, and Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 2 additional senators
for.what_they_did: Added their names as cosponsors after introduction, bringing the total to five.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on September 28, 2022, and took no further action; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill or acted to advance it.

sides.party_line_note: All five cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent, with no Republican support, and the Democratic-controlled HELP Committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

industries.industry: Website-dependent businesses (retail, services, and government-facing platforms)
industries.note: The bill would have required them to build and maintain accessible sites, with compensatory and punitive damages and attorney's fees available to disabled users who sued. Their interest in avoiding that cost runs against the disabled users the bill was meant to protect. [S3]

industries.industry: Web and software development firms ('commercial providers')
industries.note: They would face direct legal liability for delivering inaccessible products, but the same mandate creates paid demand for accessible design work and technical assistance. [S3]

industries.industry: Digital accessibility consultants and assistive technology makers
industries.note: Uniform standards and the funded technical assistance center would create a market for accessibility auditing, training, and tools, which in turn serve the disabled users relying on them. [S3]
